what_its_for: Luliconazole is an antifungal cream used to treat fungal skin infections. It is approved to treat athlete's foot (tinea pedis), jock itch (tinea cruris), and ringworm (tinea corporis) in adults. It works by killing the fungus that causes these infections.
how_to_take: Luliconazole is a cream that you apply directly to the affected skin area and a small border of skin around it. Wash and dry the affected area before applying. Use your fingertips to apply a thin layer of cream. Wash your hands after applying unless your hands are the area being treated. Apply it only to the skin — do not use it in your eyes, mouth, or vagina. Do not cover the treated area with a tight bandage unless your doctor tells you to.
dosing: Apply the cream once a day at the same time each day. For athlete's foot (between the toes), apply for 2 weeks. For athlete's foot on the bottom or sides of the foot, apply for 4 weeks. For jock itch or ringworm, apply for 1 week. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: If you miss an application, apply it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not apply extra cream to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store luliconazole cream at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep the tube tightly closed when not in use. Keep it away from heat and out of reach of children. Do not freeze the cream. Throw away any unused cream after your treatment is finished.
what_to_avoid: Avoid getting the cream in your eyes, mouth, nose, or vagina. If accidental contact occurs, rinse thoroughly with water. Avoid using tight or non-breathable clothing or footwear over the treated area, as this can make the infection worse. Do not share this medication with others. Avoid stopping the treatment early even if your symptoms improve — finish the full course to make sure the infection is completely gone.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor if: your skin becomes very red, irritated, blistered, or swollen after using the cream; your infection does not improve after a few weeks of treatment; your symptoms get worse; you develop signs of an allergic reaction such as severe rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. Seek emergency help right away if you have a serious allergic reaction.
when_it_works: You may start to notice improvement in your symptoms within the first week of treatment. However, it is important to use the cream for the full recommended time, even if you feel better sooner. The infection may come back if you stop too early. If you do not see any improvement after completing the full course, contact your doctor.
special_populations: Safety and effectiveness of luliconazole cream have not been established in children under 18 years of age, so it is generally not recommended for children unless directed by a doctor. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before using this medication. The amount of cream absorbed into your blood through the skin is very small, but it is still important to let your doctor know if you are pregnant or nursing. There are no specific dose adjustments needed for older adults, but always follow your doctor's guidance.
